t.3.77.1: Bṛhadaśva said: Having stayed there a month, O Kaunteya, and having taken leave of Bhīma, the Naiṣadha set out from the city with a small retinue toward the Niṣadhas.
t.3.77.2: With a single gleaming chariot, a full sixteen elephants, fifty horses, and six hundred foot soldiers.
t.3.77.3: That high-minded lord of the earth, hastening as if making the earth tremble, entered with great speed, greatly agitated.
t.3.77.4: Then Nala, the son of Vīrasena, approached Puṣkara and said, "Let us play dice again; I have acquired much wealth."
t.3.77.5: Damayantī, and whatever other wealth I have acquired: this indeed is my stake, but yours is the kingdom, Puṣkara.
t.3.77.6: Let the game of dice begin once more: such is my firm resolve. Good fortune to you! With a single stake, we two shall wager our lives.
t.3.77.7: Having won and carried off another's property, whether it be a kingdom or riches, one must grant a return stake, for that is said to be the highest wealth.
t.3.77.9: This kingdom, which is to be enjoyed by the lineage, must be sought in one way or another, by whatever means at all; such is the precept of the elders.
t.3.77.8: If you do not wish for that game of dice, then let the dice game of battle begin; through single combat by chariot let there indeed be an end, either for you or for me, O king.
t.3.77.11: Thus addressed by the Naiṣadha, Puṣkara, as if laughing, deeming his own victory certain, replied to the lord of the earth.
t.3.77.10: Puṣkara, let your mind be set today on one of the two: either let it be with deceit at the game of dice, or in battle let the bow be bent.
t.3.77.12: By good fortune you have earned wealth to stake again, O Naiṣadha, and by good fortune Damayantī's ill deeds have come to an end. By good fortune, too, you live on, O king, together with your wife, O slayer of foes.
t.3.77.13: Adorned with this wealth that I have won, the princess of Vidarbha, Vaidarbhī, will surely wait upon me, as an Apsaras waits upon Śakra in heaven.
t.3.77.14: For I constantly think of you and wait for you, Naiṣadha, and I find no delight in gambling with a crowd of those who are no friends of mine.
t.3.77.15: But having won today the fair-hipped, blameless Damayantī, I shall have accomplished my purpose, for she is ever in my heart.
t.3.77.17: Then the king, smiling, yet with eyes copper-red with anger, said to him: "Let us two play for the stake! Why do you keep talking? Once you have won, then indeed you will talk."
t.3.77.16: Having heard those words of his, who was babbling much and without restraint, the enraged Nala wished to cut off his head with a sword.
t.3.77.19: Having defeated Puṣkara, the king, laughing, said this: "This whole kingdom is mine, undisturbed, its thorns destroyed."
t.3.77.18: Then the dice game between Puṣkara and Nala began, and with a single throw, good fortune to you, he was defeated by Nala, he who had staked his jewels, his treasury and his hoard, and even his life.
t.3.77.20: You cannot even look upon Vaidarbhī, O outcast among kings; you fool, you along with your retinue have become her slave.
t.3.77.21: That deed by which I was defeated long ago was not done by you; that deed was done by Kali, but you, fool, do not understand it. In no way shall I lay upon you a fault committed by another.
t.3.77.23: My brotherly affection for you will never forsake me. Puṣkara, you are my brother; live for a hundred years.
t.3.77.22: Live as you please; I grant you your life. And my affection for you remains just as it was, O hero, there is no doubt.
t.3.77.24: Having thus consoled his brother, Nala, whose valor was true, embraced him again and again and sent him off to his own city.
t.3.77.25: Thus consoled by the Naiṣadha, Puṣkara, with joined palms, saluted Puṇyaśloka and then replied to him, O king.
t.3.77.26: May your fame be imperishable! Live happily for ten thousand years, O king, you who grant me my life and a place to dwell.
t.3.77.27: Thus honored by the king, King Puṣkara stayed for a month and then, delighted and surrounded by his own people, set out for his own city.
t.3.77.29: Having sent Puṣkara away, wealthy and unharmed, the glorious king entered his city, which was splendidly adorned. Having entered, the lord of the Niṣadhas consoled the citizens.
t.3.77.28: With a great army, O king, and with well-disciplined attendants, he was shining in his form like the sun, O bull among men.
